notes.meaning: Adoni-zedek, the king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua completely destroyed Jericho and Ai. He also learned that the powerful city of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and lived right among them. His name meant 'lord of righteousness,' but he led the Canaanites in opposing the true God.

The king and his people were terrified because Gibeon was large, well defended, and filled with brave warriors. Unlike other cities ruled by kings, Gibeon seems to have been led by elders, yet it was as strong as any royal city. If such a mighty city surrendered to Israel, the other kingdoms knew they were in grave danger.

Adoni-zedek called on four neighboring kings from Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon to unite their armies with his. He asked them to come up and attack Gibeon for betraying the Canaanite cause and making peace with Israel. By striking Gibeon, he hoped to punish them and stop Israel from moving any deeper into the land.

The five kings joined their armies together and set up camp to lay siege to Gibeon. They are called Amorites because that was the main ruling tribe in the southern hill country. Without realizing it, their alliance gathered them into one place so the Lord could give Israel a single decisive victory.

The leaders of Gibeon sent an urgent message to Joshua at Gilgal, pleading for immediate help against the five attacking kings. They reminded Joshua that they were now his servants and had a treaty with Israel. Because they were in danger on account of their treaty, it was Israel's duty to defend them.

Joshua honored his promise and moved out from Gilgal with his best fighting men. Even though the Gibeonites had tricked Israel earlier, Joshua refused to break his word or let his new allies perish. A servant of God keeps promises even when keeping them is difficult.

The Lord spoke to Joshua before the fight and told him not to be afraid of the huge allied army. God promised that He had already handed the enemies over to Israel and that none of them could stand. This divine promise gave Joshua full confidence, but it did not make him careless or lazy.

Joshua and his troops marched all night from Gilgal, climbing steep hills for many miles to reach Gibeon. By moving quickly in the dark, they took the five kings completely by surprise. God's promise of victory spurred the army to work with all their strength rather than sit back.

The Lord threw the enemy armies into wild panic and confusion when Israel attacked. Israel defeated them with a great slaughter near Gibeon and chased the fleeing troops through the rocky pass of Beth-horon. The pursuit swept far south toward Azekah and Makkedah as the Canaanite forces fell apart.

As the enemies ran down the steep descent of Beth-horon, the Lord sent massive hailstones raining down on them from the sky. These huge stones struck down more of the fleeing soldiers than the swords of the Israelites did. The storm miraculously struck the Canaanites without harming the Israelites who were running right behind them.

In front of the entire army, Joshua prayed to the Lord and commanded the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Ajalon. He asked for this miracle under God's guidance so the army would have enough daylight to complete the rout. Speaking this command in public showed his complete trust that God would answer.

differ.view: Some evangelicals hold that God supernaturally prolonged the daylight through unusual atmospheric light or local reflection rather than stopping the earth or heavenly bodies.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the command to the sun as poetic imagery taken from an ancient war song, meaning God gave a swift and complete victory, rather than an astronomical event.

notes.meaning: The sun and moon halted their progress across the sky until Israel completely defeated their enemies. This remarkable event was also recorded in the Book of Jashar, an ancient collection of songs celebrating God's great deeds. The day stayed bright for about a full day longer, leaving no chance for the enemy to regroup in the dark.

Never had there been a day like this before or since, where the Lord listened to a man's voice to alter the course of nature in such a grand way. The victory happened because the Lord Himself was fighting for His people Israel. It proved to all surrounding nations that the God of Israel is higher than the sun and moon they worshipped.

This verse states that Joshua and all Israel returned to the base camp at Gilgal. It serves as a general summary of the whole campaign, quoted from the ancient song, because the actual return to Gilgal happened only after the battles and executions were finished. The immediate story continues with the events at Makkedah.

During the wild retreat, the five Canaanite kings slipped away and hid together inside a cave at Makkedah. Someone discovered their hiding spot and brought the news directly to Joshua. The very kings who had marched out proudly were now trapped in the dark.

Joshua told his men to roll heavy boulders across the opening of the cave and station guards there to keep the kings trapped inside. He did not want his soldiers to stop fighting just to deal with prisoners. He wisely kept first things first, securing the leaders while keeping the army focused on the main battle.

Joshua ordered the rest of his army to keep moving and chase down the enemy soldiers from behind. He warned them not to let the Canaanites escape into their walled cities, where they could rest and fight another day. He reminded them that the Lord their God had already handed the enemy over to them.

Joshua and the Israelites carried out the pursuit until the allied army was almost entirely wiped out. Only a scattered remnant of survivors managed to slip behind the gates of their fortified cities. The confederacy was crushed, and the power of the southern kings was broken.

The whole army returned without harm to Joshua at the camp in Makkedah. Not a single person dared to speak an evil word against an Israelite, showing how completely silenced and terrified the local people were. God kept His people completely safe throughout the long fight and the pursuit.

Now that the field was cleared and the army had returned, Joshua ordered the mouth of the cave to be opened. He commanded his men to bring the five captive kings out to stand before him for formal judgment. The cave that they hoped would save them had only preserved them for God's justice.
